source.title: UNLEARN Efficient Removal of Knowledge in Large Language Models

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study applies a different weight-editing method for unlearning and measures targeted-task performance and retained performance on related or other tasks. It does not test recovery attacks.
record.gate_note: The study reports task-removal and retained-task outcomes, including comparisons with gradient ascent, KGA, and KU. It reports no fine-tuning recovery attack, activation-direction ablation, quantization attack, or prompting-only recovery. LEARN results concern adding task information, not recovering information after unlearning. Rank choices are experimental conditions, not results to treat as outcomes by themselves.
record.test_reason: The paper proposes a new weight-subtraction unlearning method (UNLEARN) for Llama 2 70b. It measures whether target-task accuracy falls while other tasks are kept, against GA, KGA and KU. This bears on the forgetting and retention parts of version A. It runs no recovery attack (fine-tuning, ablation, quantization or prompting), so the 'simple attacks don't recover it' part of A and versions B–F are untested. It is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors claim 96% forgetting with other tasks within 2.5%, and for similar tasks ~80% forgetting with the similar task within 10%. They say this far outpaces GA/KGA/KU. They acknowledge failure when one task's subspace contains another's (arithmetic/GSM8K). Their text claims 'no degradation' for discrimination applied to arithmetic, but Table 1 shows arithmetic 0.991→0.825. They do not test recovery.
record.recipe_differences: UNLEARN identifies task-specific matrices layer by layer, discriminates between task subspaces, and subtracts the modified task matrix from model weights. The study does not apply gradient ascent, Who's Harry Potter, or RMU as its proposed method.
record.method_sensitivity: Rank affects removal and related-task performance: the paper reports lower-rank experiments are less effective and cause greater degradation on the similar task. It also reports task overlap matters, with arithmetic and GSM8K especially difficult to discriminate.
record.peer_reviewed: North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The paper measures benchmark task performance rather than recovery after attacks; chance levels are not stated. It reports no uncertainty estimates. Several conclusions concern task-level metrics rather than specific facts or knowledge items, and the authors note limitations when tasks overlap.
record.rows_left_out: None. Table 1 and Table 2 outcomes relevant to targeted-task removal and retained-task performance are represented; LEARN and LoRA results are omitted because they add knowledge rather than test recovery after unlearning.

untested.parts: Whether simple attacks (relearning, prompting, quantization, ablation) recover the removed task. Also the removal of specific facts or hazardous knowledge rather than whole benchmark tasks.
All: no relearning or fine-tuning of unlearned models.
All: no activation ablation or block-vs-delete analysis of the unlearned model.
All: no quantization of unlearned weights.
All: no rephrasing, jailbreak, multilingual or in-context recovery.
All: no robustness of UNLEARN to any recovery attack is tested.

record.verdict_notes: Classed as a test of A only for its forgetting and retention parts; it could arguably be T4-like (a method paper) since no attack is run. Comparator rows are the authors' own runs of other methods and bear on A as unlearning outcomes. Table 2 rows at k=16 duplicate Table 1. LEARN results (Llama 2 7b, LegalBench) are knowledge addition and correctly excluded. No uncertainty estimates; chance levels are not stated, but generative QA and math floors are ~0.

versions.untested_parts: Tests targeted-task performance after removal and performance on other tasks, but not whether simple attacks recover the targeted knowledge. It does not establish that performance is near chance, as chance levels are not stated.
No relearning or fine-tuning attack on an already-unlearned model.
No activation-direction ablation or test of whether an attack can restore the knowledge. The paper’s weight-subspace account is not a recovery test.
No prompt rephrasing, jailbreak, language, or in-context recovery test.
No test of resistance to the recovery attacks listed in the claim.
